 "export.note":1400,"footer.dataFrom":530,"footer.partnerNote":1400,
}
for key,val in budgets.items():
    pat = re.compile(r'(  "'+re.escape(key)+r'": \{\n(?:    probe: "[^"]*",\n)?    maxWidthPx: )\d+(,\n)')
    s2 = pat.sub(lambda m: m.group(1)+str(val)+m.group(2), s, count=1)
    assert s2 != s, key
    s = s2

# Three verdict words that did not fit the 104px status column.
for old,new in [
  ('    en: "Scheduled!",\n    he: "נקבע!",\n    ru: "В плане!",\n    ja: "予定に入れました",',
   '    en: "Scheduled!",\n    he: "נקבע!",\n    ru: "В плане!",\n    ja: "予定済み",'),
  ('    en: "Outside your hours",\n    he: "מחוץ לשעות שלכם",\n    ru: "Вне ваших часов",\n    ja: "時間帯の外",',
   '    en: "Outside hours",\n    he: "מחוץ לשעות",\n    ru: "Вне часов",\n    ja: "時間帯の外",'),
]:
    assert s.count(old)==1, old[:40]
    s=s.replace(old,new)

old=''' * - `maxWidthPx` — how wide, in CSS pixels, the rendered string may be. This is
 *   XLIFF 1.2's `maxwidth` attribute, whose own `size-unit` defaults to
 *   `pixel`; it is a property of the SLOT, so it is one number for all four
 *   languages rather than one per language. The number is the narrowest the
 *   slot ever is across the layouts the page supports — both committed
 *   viewports, both directions — so a string that fits it fits everywhere.
 *   `19.6`'s case measures every string against it in the real page, so a
 *   budget is enforced rather than advisory; raising one is a claim about the
 *   design and belongs with a change to the design.'''
new=''' * - `maxWidthPx` — how wide, in CSS pixels, the rendered string may draw. This
 *   is XLIFF 1.2's `maxwidth` attribute, whose own `size-unit` defaults to
 *   `pixel`; it is a property of the SLOT, so it is one number for all four
 *   languages rather than one per language, and it is taken from the tightest
 *   layout the page supports (the narrower of the two committed viewports;
 *   direction does not change how wide a run of text draws). A slot that
 *   cannot wrap — a pill in the grid's 104px status column, a nav item, a
 *   chip — budgets that column's width, less whatever the markup puts beside
 *   the words. A slot that wraps budgets its width times the number of lines
 *   the design gives it, since a paragraph's width is its total advance spread
 *   down the block. Leaf 19.6's case measures every string against the number
 *   in the real page, so a budget is enforced rather than advisory; raising
 *   one is a claim about the design and belongs with a change to the design.'''
assert s.count(old)==1
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,"w",encoding="utf-8").write(s)
print("ok")
PY

place without touching a single component. One gradient, no images. */

# The static-website pack's keys — every repo-specific value the vendored release
# pipeline reads. Explicit on purpose: nothing here is published, versioned,
# built or tested except what this file names.
#
# The site is served from the repo root, so the publish set is the part of the
# root that IS the site. Everything else at the root is how the site is MADE:
# scraper/, docs/, design-concepts/, product-wiki/, plan/design/, scripts/ and
# the agent tooling were all served by the whole-root upload this replaces, and
# are deliberately absent here.
publish_root=.

# Named in four groups: the pages and their icons; the shared code and styles;
# each planner's own paths; and the data the browser actually fetches.
#
# The code DIRECTORIES are named as directories, not file by file, and that is a
# considered trade: a file-by-file list is exact but silently breaks the site the
# day someone adds js/foo.js and forgets this file, while a directory keeps
# working. The cost is that js/__tests__, shared/__tests__ and plan/lib/__tests__
# ride along — a few KB of harmless test code on a public site, which is the
# cheaper of the two failures.
#
# The data entries are the opposite: named file by file, because the two biggest
# files under data/ are scraper INPUTS that no page ever fetches, and shipping
# them is 10.3 MB of nothing. Excluded on purpose, verified against the fetch
# call sites in js/app.js and plan/plan.js:
#   data/normalized/shows.json  7.4M  the uncompacted master; the planner loads
#                                     shows.min.json instead
#   data/prices.json            2.9M  the scraper's price cache, already folded
#                                     into the catalogue before it ships
# The Jerusalem planner's whole catalogue is one 52 KB file, so it is named the
# same way; its raw page cache is git-ignored and never reaches this list.
publish_paths=.nojekyll index.html accessibility.html privacy.html terms.html favicon.ico favicon.svg apple-touch-icon.png css js shared package.json plan/index.html plan/plan.css plan/plan.js plan/lib plan2 planJerusalem data/venues.json data/jerusalem/shows.json data/days data/normalized/shows.min.json data/normalized/availability.min.json data/normalized/descriptions.min.json

# package.json is the single source of truth; the debug pill fetches it to show
# the running version, which is why it is in the publish set above too.
version_files=package.json

# Stamps js/build-info.js and injects the analytics beacon token — the two inline
# steps the hand-rolled deploy did, now a script that also runs on every pull
# request instead of only on a deploy.
build_command=bash scripts/build-site.sh

# The repo's own gate: unit tests, JS/Python syntax, the normalizer self-test.
# The same script the pre-commit hook runs.
test_command=bash scripts/verify.sh

# The Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon token. Public by nature — it ships to every
# visitor in the page — so it is a repo VARIABLE, never a secret, which is also
# the only kind of value the pipeline will export into a build.
build_vars=CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN

The festival planner speaks four languages, both directions, either theme

Every string the page's own chrome renders now comes from one keyed
catalogue — English, Hebrew, Russian and Japanese — written in ICU
MessageFormat and formatted by a small formatter over Intl.PluralRules,

text stays in the source's Hebrew whatever the chrome speaks.

`maxwidth`, whose own size-unit defaults to pixel — taken from the tightest
layout the page supports. The header gains the two controls that choose the
language and the theme; `lang`, `dir` and the colour scheme follow, the
board and the date window's overlay mirror for right-to-left, and both
choices are remembered under the festival's own storage prefix.

Refs #729

input.title: planJerusalem: four languages, both directions, light and dark, with a checked pixel budget per string
input.body:
Closes #729

The festival planner's own chrome now speaks **English, Hebrew, Russian and Japanese**, mirrors for right-to-left, and follows the device's light or dark scheme with a toggle to override it. The programme's own text stays in the source's Hebrew whatever the chrome speaks.

## How the translations are done

- **One keyed catalogue**, `planJerusalem/i18n/translations.js`, key-major so a key's four takes and the room it has to fit in are read together. It converts mechanically to locale-major files or to XLIFF.
- **ICU MessageFormat** patterns — the syntax every mainstream toolchain reads — formatted at runtime by `planJerusalem/i18n/format.js` (~100 lines over `Intl.PluralRules`). MessageFormat 2 is stable in Unicode LDML but `Intl.MessageFormat` is still a [TC39 stage-2 proposal](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-intl-messageformat), so no browser can format either for us and a dependency-free formatter is ours to carry.
- **Dates and numbers via `Intl`**, with a regioned tag per language (`en-GB`, so English still reads "18 Oct"), so no month or weekday name is in the catalogue at all.
- Markup binds strings with `data-i18n` / `data-i18n-<attr>`; `data-i18n-slot` marks where the page's own code writes one, which is what the pixel check measures.

## The "max pixel length" field

Each key carries `maxWidthPx` — this is [XLIFF 1.2's `maxwidth`](https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/v1.2/os/xliff-core.html), whose own `size-unit` **defaults to pixel**, so the field the request asked for is the one the localisation standard already has.

A letter becomes pixels by **measuring, not by a rule of our own**: leaf `19.6`'s case drives the real page under the harness's pinned Chromium and, for every key, builds a probe carrying that key's slot's own resolved typography, sets the string, and reads the box back — in all four languages and at **both committed viewports**. The number a translator is given is the number the browser holds them to.

Where the numbers come from: a slot that cannot wrap budgets its column (the grid's status column is 104px, less the mark the markup puts beside the words — three verdict words were shortened to fit); a slot that wraps budgets its narrowest width times the lines the design gives it. Keys with no box at all — an `aria-label`, an OS-drawn `title`, the document title — carry `maxWidthPx: null` plus a stated reason, rather than a `0` pretending to be a measurement.

**On "the plan pages are only desktop"**: they respond (940px and 520px breakpoints) and the harness has a mobile viewport, so the budgets are the tighter of the two. Adding two header controls did overflow the header at 390px — that is fixed here, and the page now has no horizontal overflow at that width.

## Checks

- `19.5` (default lane, `npm test`): every key in every language, no empty strings, no stray fields, a budget or a stated reason, the same arguments in every language, every plural category the language's own CLDR data requires, every pattern formats, no key the page never names, no binding the catalogue lacks.
- `19.6` (UI lane): the measurement above, plus a guard that every Japanese character is covered by a vendored Noto Sans JP chunk — the harness's font jail carries no CJK, so an uncovered character would measure and render as tofu.

## Goldens

New: the whole page in Hebrew RTL (`19.1`), the whole page in dark mode (`19.2`), the Russian and Japanese chrome (`19.3`). Whole-page captures are deliberate for the first two: what they assert is that the layout holds, which no crop shows.

**Two committed goldens need re-baselining and I have not touched them** — `jerusalem-chrome.18.1` (the header gained the language picker and the theme toggle) and `jerusalem-schedule.18.5` (6 pixels of ±1 at two rounded corners, from `light-dark()` colours blending a shade differently). Asking the owner before refreshing, per the approval contract. Every other golden in the suite is untouched and green (113 pass).

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- deterministic-expecteds: What makes a rendered expected byte-stable — the pinned clock, faked inputs, real fonts, fixed-duration pumps — and the per-stack rendering recipe (jsdom+satori for DOM products, Flutter golden files) with pixel-exact comparison. Use when writing a case, the render harness or the fake world under dev/requirements.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- explore-link: Mine one given URL for product, market, usage and pricing insights and fold them into an existing product-wiki page — cited, dated, delivered as a PR. Use when the owner says "/explore-link <url>", or hands over a link and asks for it to be read into the wiki.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

lines: -  <meta name="description" content="How EdFringeNow works with keyboards, screen readers and reduced motion — and how to tell us when it doesn't." />

-

We want EdFringeNow to be usable by everyone — on a phone, on a street, in a hurry.

-
  • Full keyboard navigation, with a clearly visible focus outline on every control.

-
  • Semantic markup and ARIA labels, so a screen reader can announce the plan, the filters, and the list of shows.

-
  • Respects your device's “reduce motion” setting — animations switch off when you ask them to.

-
  • Large tap targets and a single, legible column that scales down to small screens.

-

We aim to meet WCAG 2.1 AA. We're a small project and we won't always hit it perfectly.

-

input.body:
Closes #729

The festival planner's own chrome now speaks **English, Hebrew, Russian and Japanese**, mirrors for right-to-left, and follows the device's light or dark scheme with a toggle to override it. The programme's own text stays in the source's Hebrew whatever the chrome speaks.

Rebased onto the `site/` move (#731); the page lives at `site/planJerusalem/` and its catalogue at `site/planJerusalem/i18n/`.

## How the translations are done

- **One keyed catalogue**, `site/planJerusalem/i18n/translations.js`, key-major so a key's four takes and the room it has to fit in are read together. It converts mechanically to locale-major files or to XLIFF.
- **ICU MessageFormat** patterns — the syntax every mainstream toolchain reads — formatted at runtime by `site/planJerusalem/i18n/format.js` (~100 lines over `Intl.PluralRules`). MessageFormat 2 is stable in Unicode LDML but `Intl.MessageFormat` is still a [TC39 stage-2 proposal](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-intl-messageformat), so no browser can format either for us and a dependency-free formatter is ours to carry.
- **Dates and numbers via `Intl`**, with a regioned tag per language (`en-GB`, so English still reads "18 Oct"), so no month or weekday name is in the catalogue at all.
- Markup binds strings with `data-i18n` / `data-i18n-<attr>`; `data-i18n-slot` marks where the page's own code writes one, which is what the pixel check measures.

## The "max pixel length" field

Each key carries `maxWidthPx` — this is [XLIFF 1.2's `maxwidth`](https://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/v1.2/os/xliff-core.html), whose own `size-unit` **defaults to pixel**, so the field the request asked for is the one the localisation standard already has.

A letter becomes pixels by **measuring, not by a rule of our own**: leaf `19.6`'s case drives the real page under the harness's pinned Chromium and, for every key, builds a probe carrying that key's slot's own resolved typography, sets the string, and reads the box back — in all four languages and at **both committed viewports**. The number a translator is given is the number the browser holds them to.

Where the numbers come from: a slot that cannot wrap budgets its column (the grid's status column is 104px, less the mark the markup puts beside the words — three verdict words were shortened to fit); a slot that wraps budgets its narrowest width times the lines the design gives it. Keys with no box at all — an `aria-label`, an OS-drawn `title`, the document title — carry `maxWidthPx: null` plus a stated reason, rather than a `0` pretending to be a measurement.

**On "the plan pages are only desktop"**: they respond (940px and 520px breakpoints) and the harness has a mobile viewport, so the budgets are the tighter of the two. Adding two header controls did overflow the header at 390px — that is fixed here, and the page now has no horizontal overflow at that width.

## Checks

- `19.5` (default lane, `npm test`): every key in every language, no empty strings, no stray fields, a budget or a stated reason, the same arguments in every language, every plural category the language's own CLDR data requires, every pattern formats, no key the page never names, no binding the catalogue lacks.
- `19.6` (UI lane): the measurement above, plus a guard that every Japanese character is covered by a vendored Noto Sans JP chunk — the harness's font jail carries no CJK, so an uncovered character would measure and render as tofu.

## Goldens

New: the whole page in Hebrew RTL (`19.1`), the whole page in dark mode (`19.2`), the Russian and Japanese chrome (`19.3`). Whole-page captures are deliberate for the first two: what they assert is that the layout holds, which no crop shows.

Two committed goldens were **re-baselined**, surfaced to the owner first: `jerusalem-chrome.18.1` (the header gained the language picker and the theme toggle — the intended change) and `jerusalem-schedule.18.5` (six pixels of ±1 where two rounded corners are antialiased, which is what reading those colours through `light-dark()` costs). Every other golden in the suite is untouched.

after.description: Cursor for pagination, used only by the get_review_comments method. Pass the endCursor from the previous page's PageInfo to fetch the next page.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); when the change has an issue,
   the body carries `Closes #<issue>` on its own line.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --pr <pr>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --pr <pr>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
   again. (1)
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read an issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
